title: Observation of lepton-number violation

concept.text: The innovation is a convincing laboratory observation that lepton number can change, pursued here through neutrinoless double beta decay. In this hypothetical nuclear decay, a candidate nucleus emits two electrons without the two antineutrinos that accompany ordinary double beta decay. The process would change lepton number by two units. Its experimental signature would be a peak in the summed energy of the electrons at the nucleus’s decay energy, or Q-value, above a characterized background.

A securely identified observation would imply a Majorana component of neutrino mass: neutrinos could not be described exclusively as Dirac particles with a conserved distinction between particle and antiparticle. However, identifying the decay would not by itself establish which microscopic process dominates its rate. Interpreting a measured half-life as an effective Majorana neutrino mass requires an assumed decay mechanism and calculations of the relevant nuclear matrix elements.

significance.text: A confirmed observation would fundamentally revise the lepton sector by establishing a process that violates lepton-number conservation and implies Majorana neutrino character. The direct advance would be experimental evidence about a basic symmetry and the nature of neutrino mass. It would not require agreement on the decay’s cosmological implications to be a major discovery.

The discovery could inform explanations of why the universe contains more matter than antimatter, including leptogenesis. That connection is conditional: an observed decay would not establish the particles, interactions or early-universe history responsible for the cosmic matter excess. Further evidence would be needed to connect the laboratory process to a successful cosmological mechanism, and to determine whether light-neutrino exchange explains the measured decay rate.

Impact assessment: the revolutionary consequence would be new knowledge of fundamental physics. No immediate technology follows from the proposed observation, and neither a practical application nor a complete explanation of the cosmic matter excess should be treated as an assured downstream outcome.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is to identify an exceptionally rare neutrinoless decay securely enough to distinguish it from background events and instrumental effects. The documented germanium searches have measured backgrounds and set half-life limits without finding evidence for a signal. Reaching a theoretically motivated mass range with an exclusion limit would remain a constraint on the process, rather than an observation.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing search must combine sufficient isotope exposure with precise energy measurement, stable calibration and strong rejection of backgrounds. The central difficulty is retaining genuine candidate decays while suppressing or characterizing events that could populate the same energy region. A peak’s location alone is insufficient: the experiment must also establish that a background line, detector response or analysis artifact cannot plausibly explain it. Larger exposure only improves the discovery opportunity when the background and detector performance remain controlled.

A separate scientific barrier is interpreting the rate. The effective Majorana mass inferred under Majorana-neutrino mediation depends on nuclear matrix elements; other possible decay mechanisms complicate that interpretation further. Measurements in different isotopes must therefore be compared through their isotope-dependent phase space and nuclear response under an explicitly stated mechanism. Equal half-lives across isotopes are not expected or required.

current_state.text: The supplied review verifies that LEGEND-200’s first search used 61.0 kg yr of germanium-76 exposure. Its combination with GERDA and the MAJORANA DEMONSTRATOR incorporated a further 127.2 kg yr and 64.5 kg yr, respectively, for 252.7 kg yr in total. The combined analysis found no evidence for a signal, reporting a background-only p-value of 0.29 and a half-life lower limit of T1/2 > 1.9 × 10^26 years at 90% confidence. Its median sensitivity was 2.8 × 10^26 years; that expected sensitivity is distinct from the observed limit. The result is documented in the 2025 arXiv paper and was described in LBNL’s 30 March 2026 publication summary.

Assuming Majorana-neutrino mediation, the germanium analysis reports an effective Majorana mass bound of 75–200 meV for its adopted range of nuclear matrix elements. It also reports a separate Bayesian estimate of 320 meV using an ab initio nuclear calculation. These are conditional interpretations of the null result, rather than measurements of a neutrino mass. The separate estimate should not be silently folded into the 75–200 meV range because it uses a different nuclear calculation and statistical treatment.

LBNL’s March 2026 summary describes the combined half-life limit as world-leading for germanium-76. This is an isotope-specific claim, not a demonstrated ranking over xenon experiments. Moreover, a larger numerical half-life limit in a different isotope does not by itself establish stronger sensitivity to a common particle-physics parameter; such a comparison requires a mechanism and isotope-dependent nuclear calculations.

The reconciled research attributes to KamLAND-Zen a complete 800-phase xenon-136 exposure of 2.1 ton yr and, after combination with an earlier phase, a null result with T1/2 > 3.8 × 10^26 years at 90% confidence and an effective Majorana mass bound of 28–122 meV. It identifies the publication as Physical Review Letters 135, 262501, dated 29 December 2025. However, the source index contains no captured text for that source, and the supplied review could not verify these numbers or publication details. They remain reported research claims, not independently validated results in this record. The research also rejects a 4.3 × 10^26-year figure attributed to a 2024 talk, but the supplied evidence cannot resolve that historical comparison. Missing source material does not establish that either reported figure is false.

The LEGEND program describes a future discovery-sensitivity goal beyond 10^28 years. LBNL’s 30 March 2026 account states that LEGEND-1000 completed a CD-1 independent project review in November 2025 and was awaiting final DOE CD-1 approval. Completing that review was neither final approval nor completion of the experiment, and the projected sensitivity was not an achieved search result.

The supported searches described here report no observation. The supplied materials contain no fresh worldwide search establishing the discovery status or strongest available limit as of 1 November 2026. The review had complete extracted LEGEND paper prose and the complete LBNL article, while the arXiv landing page supplied only abstract-level evidence. Garbled figure labels in the paper extraction limited figure-based interpretation; the review relied on readable prose for the numerical results. These limitations leave the dated germanium findings intact while restricting claims about global rankings and subsequent developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed discovery demonstration: a signal peak at the Q-value with at least 5σ significance in one isotope, supported by calibrated energy response, validated signal identification and a background model constrained by sidebands and relevant control measurements. The assessment should test plausible background-line and instrumental explanations, rather than relying only on the peak’s energy or statistical significance. The 5σ threshold and this package of checks are proposed criteria for this record, not an established requirement prescribed by the supplied paper.
completion_criteria.label: Validated Q-value peak reaches 5σ after testing alternative explanations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed independent confirmation: reproduce the signal in an independent detector using the same isotope, or observe a compatible signal in a second isotope. Same-isotope measurements should infer compatible half-lives after accounting for uncertainties. Different-isotope measurements should instead show rates compatible with an explicitly stated decay mechanism and its nuclear uncertainties; their half-lives need not be equal. Reproducibility should include enough calibration, background and analysis information to allow meaningful independent scrutiny.
completion_criteria.label: Independent detector or second isotope reproduces a compatible signal

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: a lower half-life limit or an excess below the chosen discovery threshold would not complete the demonstration. A securely identified neutrinoless double beta decay would establish lepton-number violation without first resolving its cosmological role, but would not automatically identify the dominant decay mechanism. Confirmation in a finite set of detectors and isotopes would establish demonstrated reproducibility and breadth for those cases, rather than universal decay behavior across all nuclei.
completion_criteria.label: State discovery boundaries and limits on mechanism and reproducibility

related_concepts.text: PHY-13, A tested mechanism for the cosmic matter excess, overlaps through the possible role of lepton-number violation in leptogenesis. PHY-08 concerns establishing a laboratory process; PHY-13 requires a tested account of how the cosmic asymmetry arose. Observing neutrinoless double beta decay could constrain or motivate such accounts without completing PHY-13.

Roster distinction: PHY-07, Observation of baryon-number violation, concerns violation of the quantum number associated with baryons. PHY-08 concerns lepton number and the neutrino sector. Both would test fundamental conservation laws, and theoretical explanations may connect them, but an observation of neutrinoless double beta decay would not itself establish baryon-number violation. They remain separate innovations with separate experimental completion conditions.

unresolved_issues: KamLAND-Zen’s reported 2.1 ton yr exposure, 3.8 × 10^26-year limit, 28–122 meV interpretation and December 2025 publication details remain unverified because no source text was captured.
The relationship between the reported 2024 talk figure of 4.3 × 10^26 years and the research’s claimed published value of 3.8 × 10^26 years remains unresolved.
The strongest worldwide result and observation status as of 1 November 2026 are not established by the supplied evidence; LEGEND-1000’s status after the March 2026 account is also unknown.
The dominant decay mechanism and applicable nuclear matrix elements would remain interpretation questions even after a discovery; the reported mass bounds do not resolve them.
The proposed 5σ threshold and confirmation policy are record-specific proposals. The supplied sources do not establish them as a universally adopted discovery standard.

The arXiv landing page and paper PDF reportedly differ in a background unit. No background-index number is adopted here, so the discrepancy does not alter the retained exposure, half-life or sensitivity results.

brief.title: Catching a decay that breaks a basic rule of matter
possible: Scientists could catch an atomic nucleus releasing a pair of electrons without the usual antineutrinos. Antineutrinos are the antimatter counterparts of neutrinos, particles with mass. This decay would reveal that neutrinos cannot have a completely separate identity from their antimatter counterparts.
why: For physicists, the discovery would change the rules describing matter. It would show that lepton number—the balance between particles such as electrons and neutrinos and their antimatter counterparts—can change.
It could also help scientists investigate why the universe contains more matter than antimatter.

sources.cited_for: It supports the case that searches using xenon have constrained the decay without observing it.
sources.not_established: The reported search does not establish an observation.

shown: The LEGEND collaboration combined germanium measurements from its experiment, GERDA and the MAJORANA DEMONSTRATOR. It found no signal and placed a lower limit of 1.9 × 10^26 years on the half-life—the time in which half the candidate nuclei would decay through this process.
missing: A convincing concentration of events at the expected total electron energy has yet to be observed.
An observed signal must survive tests of background radiation, detector response and analysis errors.
An independent detector or another suitable form of an element must reproduce a compatible signal.

milestones.label: A convincing signal survives alternative explanations
milestones.explanation: A peak at the expected energy would have to reach 5σ, a statistical discovery threshold, with calibrated detectors and tested background explanations. This would distinguish a decay signal from a misleading excess.

milestones.label: An independent experiment finds a compatible signal
milestones.explanation: An independent detector or a second isotope, a form of an element, would have to find a compatible signal. Agreement would establish reproducibility, allowing for how different nuclei respond under a stated decay mechanism.

milestones.label: The discovery's meaning and limits are stated
milestones.explanation: The claim would have to distinguish a discovery from a limit or weaker excess and state what remains unknown about its cause and reproducibility. This would keep the conclusion within what the experiments demonstrate.

uncertain: Even after discovery, the process driving the decay and the nuclear calculations needed to infer neutrino mass could remain uncertain.
The proposed statistical threshold and independent confirmation policy are not a universally established discovery standard.
A laboratory observation would not by itself explain the universe's excess of matter over antimatter.

page.title: Observation of neutrinoless double beta decay
page.definition: A nucleus is observed to emit two electrons without antineutrinos, with their summed energy equal to the nuclear decay energy. This changes lepton number—the number of leptons minus antileptons—by two units and establishes a Majorana component of neutrino mass, which permits neutrino–antineutrino conversion.

goal.need: Neutrino oscillations establish mass but leave its Majorana character unresolved. KamLAND-Zen’s null search constrains the effective Majorana mass, the coherent electron-flavour neutrino mass combination, to below 28–122 meV across its adopted nuclear calculations. NSAC’s discovery-sensitivity target is 15 meV. These mass interpretations assume light-Majorana-neutrino exchange; observing the decay would establish lepton-number violation without that assumption.

completion.title: A validated neutrinoless double beta decay signal excludes background alone at 99.73% confidence.
completion.criterion: Observe a signal at the candidate nucleus’s decay energy that excludes the background-only hypothesis at 99.73% confidence, the double-beta-decay field’s two-sided-Gaussian 3σ convention. Establish its validity through calibrated detector performance and demonstrated understanding of backgrounds and analysis procedures, following NSAC’s standard of proof. This test concerns observed events; projected discovery sensitivity and half-life exclusion limits do not satisfy it.
completion.set_by: Double-beta-decay discovery convention documented by Agostini and colleagues, section V.E.2 of their 2023 review; signal-validity requirements are specified in section 3 of NSAC’s 2014 report.
completion.threshold_quote:
the C.L. required
for a discovery is equivalent to excluding 3σ two-sided
fluctuation of a Gaussian random variable
completion.basis: The review explicitly identifies this confidence level as the field’s discovery convention. NSAC’s 2015 report documents adoption of a common 3σ sensitivity benchmark; its 2014 standard of proof additionally requires an experiment to establish its signal’s validity. This is a documented convention rather than a universally binding discovery protocol.

milestones.title: A candidate isotope’s two-neutrino double beta decay is detected by direct counting.
milestones.criterion: Directly detect the allowed decay into two electrons and two antineutrinos and determine its nonzero decay rate. The first laboratory demonstration used selenium-82 in 1987. Barabash’s 2020 evaluation records positive counting measurements for every tracked case; example useful-event yields are 25,690 for germanium-76, about 19,000 for xenon-136, about 20,000 for tellurium-130 and 35,638 for molybdenum-100.
milestones.set_by: Direct-observation convention documented in Moe’s historical account and Barabash’s experimental evaluation; the original laboratory demonstration concerned selenium-82.
milestones.threshold_quote: a definitive laboratory observation of two-neutrino ββ decay, in August 1987.

milestones.title: An isotope search expects fewer than one background event over its design exposure.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a measured background rate implying fewer than one expected background count in the stated signal window over the design exposure. GERDA demonstrated this for germanium-76 at 100 kg·year design exposure. CUPID-Mo reported a background-free measurement with zero signal-window events in 1.47 kg·year of molybdenum-100. The cited KamLAND-Zen xenon-136 and CUORE tellurium-130 datasets have background contributions exceeding this threshold. This performance milestone is optional for discovery.
milestones.set_by: GERDA Collaboration’s published definition of a background-free search, originally stated for germanium-76; this performance test can be applied separately to other isotopes.
milestones.threshold_quote:
The expected background
is less than one count in the energy region of interest up
to the design exposure

milestones.title: An isotope search reaches 3σ discovery sensitivity at an effective Majorana mass of 15 meV.
milestones.criterion: Within 10 live-years, accumulate data giving a 50% probability of a 99.73%-confidence discovery at 15 meV, assuming light-Majorana exchange and the lowest viable nuclear matrix elements. Cited null searches give half-life lower limits: germanium-76, 1.9 × 10²⁶ years from 61.0 kg·year plus earlier data; xenon-136, 3.8 × 10²⁶ years from 2.1 tonne·year plus earlier data; tellurium-130, 3.5 × 10²⁵ years from 567.0 kg·year; molybdenum-100, 1.8 × 10²⁴ years from 1.47 kg·year. Germanium/xenon limits use 90% confidence; tellurium/molybdenum use 90% credibility. These results do not establish the target sensitivity.
milestones.set_by: DOE/NSF Nuclear Science Advisory Committee, 2014 neutrinoless double beta decay report, section 3, discovery-potential guideline; the target applies separately to each isotope.
